Big Question
Today’s Wonder

Ransom only goes to The Rise because he promised a worried mother he would. Is a small promise worth keeping when keeping it costs you?

🎯
Objectives
By the end of this lesson…
🔭Context: I will place Lewis’s novel in the long line of voyage-to-another-world stories and say what he owes to H. G. Wells.
📖Reading: I will explain what Ransom’s promise shows about him and spot a hint of things to come (foreshadowing).
🔤Words: I will learn five words from Chapters 1 and 2.
🗝️Characters: I will read each man’s perspective, his attitude toward other people, in what he does and says.
✏️Writing: I will punctuate an appositive and copy a sentence exactly, then say what one mark in it does.

📜 The Author’s Note
Lewis, at the front of the book
Note · front of the book
“The author would be sorry if any reader supposed he was too stupid to have enjoyed Mr H. G. Wells’s fantasies or too ungrateful to acknowledge his debt to them.”
The genre itself. The voyage through space and the strange world at the end of it. Wells sent Martians to England and two Englishmen to the Moon, and Lewis says plainly that he enjoyed those stories and owes them a debt.
The chips from the timeline. The same note says the “slighting references” to earlier stories of this kind are there “for purely dramatic purposes.” In The War of the Worlds, two worlds meet in invasion and terror. Lewis is about to put that expectation to the test.
Predict one thing Lewis will do differently from a story where the aliens are monsters.

✏️ Fix the Sentence
Capitals and commas
✅ Correct model
Professor Lovelore, a scholar of old stories, began the lesson.

Words that rename a noun, such as a scholar of old stories, are called an appositive. Commas set the appositive off from the rest of the sentence, on both sides. Names of particular people and places start with a capital letter. Use the model to fix the sentence below.

Ulysses
Alfred, Lord Tennyson (1842) · Lines 1–17 of 70
It little profits that an idle king, By this still hearth, among these barren crags, Match’d with an aged wife, I mete and dole Unequal laws unto a savage race, That hoard, and sleep, and feed, and know not me. I cannot rest from travel: I will drink Life to the lees: all times I have enjoy’d Greatly, have suffer’d greatly, both with those That loved me, and alone; on shore, and when Thro’ scudding drifts the rainy Hyades Vext the dim sea: I am become a name; For always roaming with a hungry heart Much have I seen and known; cities of men And manners, climates, councils, governments, Myself not least, but honour’d of them all; And drunk delight of battle with my peers, Far on the ringing plains of windy Troy.
mete and dole: measure out and hand out · lees: the dregs at the bottom of a cup · Hyades: a cluster of stars said to bring rain · vext: troubled · peers: equals, fellow warriors · Troy: the city the Greeks besieged for ten years

🎓 Questions from Professor Lovelore
She asks. You answer.
0 / 3
Professor Lovelore
Here is my first question. Ransom is tired, he has been turned away from an inn, and at the gate he would rather walk on to Sterk. Yet he goes in. What does that show about him?
Your answer
Professor Lovelore
Next question. Over his drink, Devine asked Ransom a string of questions. Does anyone know where he is? Does he have a wife, a parent, an address? What were those questions really for?
Your answer
Professor Lovelore
Last question. After Ransom is drugged he has a dream of a walled garden. Lewis says Ransom “could never be sure” whether the dream has any bearing on the events of the book. What does that doubt do to you as a reader?
Your answer
Professor Lovelore

Good. Look at what your answers share. A promise pulls Ransom through a gate he did not want to open. A friendly voice hides a calculation. A dream shows a wall, a dark side, and a door that opens from the outside.

A hint, placed early, about what will happen later is called foreshadowing. The door in the wall, and the strange people who answer “Hoo-Hoo-Hoo?” like owls, are a hint of things to come. Keep them in mind.

👂 Overheard
Who says it, and what does it show?
0 / 7
Chapter 1“We ought to have a dog in this place,”
Who says it?
Chapter 2“The boy was ideal,”
Who says it?
Chapter 2“This busybody, on the other hand, will not be missed for months,”
Who says it?
Chapter 2“He is, after all, human.”
Who says it?
Chapter 2“In a great cause -”
Who says it?
Chapter 2“Take his feet and I’ll take his head,”
Who says it?
What do the six lines show about these two men?
🔎

That is perspective: a character’s attitude toward the people around him. Lewis does not tell you what Weston and Devine think. He lets each man show it in what he says.

Jonah’s copywork
8th Grade Scholar

Sentence: He tried the gate and found it locked.

One mark: The full stop after “locked” is flat and final. Lewis does not hurry on with a comma or a dash, so the sentence shuts the way the gate does.
